For self-employed professionals and small companies, a website often looks like something that is obviously useful. But from a practical standpoint, a different question matters more: does it function as an asset, or does it simply consume money and time for maintenance? This is especially visible where the owner is personally handling clients, sales, and administration at the same time.

- The first criterion is very simple: if you were to stop advertising and external promotion today, would the website still remain useful? For example, would it continue to bring in search inquiries, collect contact details, present services clearly, save time on explanations, or simplify booking? If not, it may not yet be an asset, but rather a digital business card. And that is not necessarily bad — what matters is understanding this honestly.
- The second criterion is control. The domain, hosting, email, analytics, forms, texts, and access credentials — all of this should be under the business owner’s control. Otherwise, dependency on a contractor or an acquaintance who “set everything up at some point” can arise at any moment. For Selbständige, this is especially painful, because there is usually no spare administrative capacity.
- The third criterion is the website’s role in day-to-day operations. If it automates inquiries, bookings, answers to standard questions, data transfer into the CRM, or at least reduces the volume of manual correspondence, it is already creating real value. If, on the other hand, the website merely exists while all work still continues manually, its role should be reassessed.

How do you personally define the moment when a website stops being just an online presence and starts functioning as an asset?
